title: Do you "have" things, or are they just near you?
concept_note: Four languages, four different ways of expressing the same basic idea of possession.

entries.gloss: I have a cat. (literally: at me, there exists, a cat)
entries.note: No verb "to have" at all — possession is a location, not an action.
A dedicated possession verb (avoir), used constantly, including as a grammatical helper elsewhere.
Same structure as French — a real "to have" verb (haben), also doubling as a grammatical helper.

entries.gloss: There is a cat. (used to mean "I have a cat" when context makes the owner clear)
entries.note: No possession verb either — existence itself (いる/ある) stands in for "having," with the owner often left unsaid.

title: Does this word feel more like a "he" or a "she"?
concept_note: Three of these four languages assign every noun a gender — but the systems don't agree with each other, or even with logic.

entries.note: Two genders, largely arbitrary — no reliable ending to predict which.

entries.native: der Tisch (m), die Tür (f), das Buch (n)
entries.gloss: the table, the door, the book
entries.note: Three genders, just as arbitrary as French, plus a third option.
Three genders too, but the noun's own ending is a much more reliable clue than in French/German.
No grammatical gender at all — nouns are just nouns, full stop.

title: How does your language say "you" differently to a stranger?
concept_note: Every one of these languages marks social distance — just through a completely different piece of grammar.

entries.note: A second-person pronoun swap — pick the wrong one and it's an actual social misstep.
The exact same two-pronoun system as French, historically borrowed from it.
Same idea again, though Sie is also, confusingly, the same word as "she" and "they."

entries.native: 食べる → 召し上がる / いただく
entries.gloss: to eat → to eat (respectful) / to eat (humble)
entries.note: No pronoun swap at all — formality is instead built directly into the verb itself (keigo).

title: How much can you scramble a sentence before it breaks?
concept_note: Some languages need strict word order to know who's doing what to whom. Others barely need order at all.

entries.native: 私はりんごを食べます。
entries.note: Verb-final, but particles (は/を) mark each word's role, so order can shift somewhat since the particles carry the grammar.

entries.native: Анна читает книгу. / Книгу читает Анна.
entries.gloss: Anna is reading the book. (both orders, same meaning)
entries.note: Case endings mark subject/object directly, so word order is free to shift purely for emphasis.
Rigid verb-second rule — whatever comes first, the verb must be second, no exceptions.
Strict subject-verb-object order — reordering it doesn't just shift emphasis, it can just be wrong.

title: How many words does it take to say "no"?
concept_note: Negating a sentence looks like a small grammatical detail, but each language handles it in a completely different shape.

entries.note: Historically two pieces wrapped around the verb (ne...pas) — though casual spoken French quietly drops the ne entirely.
A single word, nicht, placed after the verb and object rather than wrapped around anything.
Just не directly before the verb — the simplest of the four.
No separate negation word at all — negation is a verb ending swap (-ません/-ない).

title: One past tense, or does the shape of the verb do the work?
concept_note: "I ate" looks like a single idea, but these four languages build it with entirely different machinery.

entries.note: Compound: avoir + past participle — an auxiliary verb doing half the work.
The same compound structure as French — haben + past participle.
A single verb form, no auxiliary — but it also encodes aspect (poel = completed the eating), not just tense.
Also no auxiliary verb — the verb ending itself swaps (-ます → -ました) to mark past tense.

title: How do you turn a statement into a question?
concept_note: Same underlying sentence, four different mechanisms for flagging "this is a question."

entries.native: Tu viens ? / Est-ce que tu viens ? / Viens-tu ?
entries.note: Three coexisting strategies: rising intonation alone, adding the est-ce que particle, or inverting subject and verb.
Just invert verb and subject — no extra particle needed.
Identical word order to the statement — only intonation (and the question mark in writing) signals it's a question.
Add the particle か to the end of the statement — nothing else in the sentence changes at all.

title: How do you show there's more than one?
concept_note: "Add an -s" is an English habit — none of these four languages actually agree on how to mark plural.

entries.note: The -s is silent — the plural is really carried by the article (le → les), not the noun's pronunciation.

entries.native: das Kind → die Kinder, der Tisch → die Tische
entries.gloss: the child → the children, the table → the tables
entries.note: Several irregular patterns (umlaut, -er, -e, -(e)n, or no change) that have to be memorized per noun.

entries.native: книга → книги, but две книги / пять книг
entries.gloss: book → books, but two books / five books
entries.note: Plural endings shift again depending on the number counting them — see the numbers-and-case oddity.
No plural marking at all — the same word covers one or many, left to context.

title: Does the describing word come before or after the thing it describes?
concept_note: Adjective placement looks trivial until you realize these languages split roughly down the middle on it.

entries.native: une voiture rouge, but une belle voiture
entries.gloss: a red car, but a beautiful car
entries.note: Most adjectives follow the noun — but a small, common set (beauty, age, goodness, size) goes before it instead.
Always before the noun, but the adjective's ending shifts with the noun's case, gender, and article.
Also always before the noun, agreeing in gender, number, and case with it.
Before the noun too — but i-adjectives like 赤い conjugate for tense/negation the same way verbs do.

title: How do you make a word sound small or affectionate?
concept_note: Making something sound "little" or dear is a live, everyday grammatical process in some of these languages — and barely exists in others.

entries.gloss: cat → little cat, Anna → a dozen affectionate variants
entries.note: An extremely productive suffix system, stackable onto nearly any noun or name.
The -chen/-lein suffixes are productive too, and always force the resulting word to be neuter — regardless of the original noun's own gender.
Diminutive suffixes (-ette, -on) exist but are far less productive — mostly fixed, individually-memorized words rather than a live rule.

entries.native: たろう → たろうちゃん
entries.note: Achieved through a name suffix (ちゃん) rather than reshaping the noun itself.

title: Can you just say the number, or does something else have to agree with it?
concept_note: Counting looks universal, but each language attaches its own extra grammatical baggage to numbers.

entries.note: You can't just say the number — a counter word tied to the object's shape or category comes with it every time.

entries.native: один стол, два стола, пять столов
entries.gloss: one table, two tables, five tables
entries.note: The number itself forces the following noun into a different case/form depending on which number it is.
A base-20 counting system still hides inside standard French for 70-99.
Units are read before tens, reversed from English's order.

title: Is the action finished, or still going — and is that baked into the verb itself?
concept_note: English leans on tense plus a few helper words for this. One of these languages builds it straight into the verb's identity.

entries.note: Verbs come in aspect pairs — completion vs. ongoing-ness is marked independently of tense, on almost every verb.

entries.gloss: eating / has eaten (depending on the verb)
entries.note: Ongoing/resultant aspect is built with a separate periphrastic form (-ている) rather than a distinct verb pair.

entries.native: je mangeais (imparfait) vs. j'ai mangé (passé composé)
entries.gloss: I was eating / used to eat vs. I ate
entries.note: No lexical aspect pairs — ongoing vs. completed is a choice between two separate past tenses instead.
No grammatical aspect marking at all — a single past tense covers both, disambiguated only by context.

title: Does a single word change meaning depending on whether something is moving or staying still?
concept_note: Talking about "in" or "at" a place sounds simple — two of these languages make the exact same preposition mean something different depending on grammar alone.

entries.native: in der Schule (dative) vs. in die Schule (accusative)
entries.gloss: in the school (staying) vs. into the school (moving)
entries.note: The same preposition, in, flips between marking static location and motion-toward purely via which case follows it.

entries.gloss: in the school (staying) vs. into the school (moving)
entries.note: Same mechanism as German — one preposition, two different cases, two different meanings.

entries.native: 学校にいる vs. 学校で勉強する
entries.gloss: to be at school vs. to study at school
entries.note: Two different particles (に vs. で) split this instead — に for existing somewhere, で for an action happening somewhere.
One invariant preposition either way — motion vs. location is disambiguated by the verb, not the preposition.

title: Is that blue, or is that a completely different color?
concept_note: Basic color vocabulary feels like a universal, physical fact — until you notice languages don't slice the color wheel the same way.

entries.note: 青 (ao) historically spans what English splits into blue and green — the "go" light is called blue even though it looks green.
Treated as two entirely separate basic colors, not shades of one "blue" — there's no single umbrella word for blue at all.
Maps onto English's basic color set fairly closely, one word per color.
Also a close one-to-one match with English's basic palette.

title: Does your word for "brother" depend on whose family, or who's older?
concept_note: "Brother" and "mother" feel like fixed, single words — some of these languages instead encode relative age or whose family you're talking about.

entries.note: The word changes depending on whether you're referring to your own family or someone else's — not just politeness, a real vocabulary split.
Formal names embed a patronymic — literally naming whose child you are, in every official reference to a person.
One flat word regardless of relative age or whose family — no built-in distinction at all.
Same as German — a single word covers the relation with no age or ownership distinction.

title: Does your language even group large numbers the same way?
concept_note: English chunks big numbers in thousands. Not every one of these four languages agrees that's the natural unit.

entries.note: Numbers group in units of 10,000 (万), not 1,000 — so large numbers are chunked and read completely differently than in English.
Written and spoken as one long compound word, with the units-before-tens reversal baked into every number above twenty.
The number-forces-noun-case rule still applies even at this size, compounding the complexity as numbers get bigger.
The base-20 leftover keeps compounding for every number in the 80s and 90s, not just round tens.
